result.summary: The Giants try to seize heaven by piling mountains up to the stars, and Jupiter strikes them down with his lightning. Earth brings their spilt blood to life as a new race of men, who prove violent and contemptuous of the gods.

scenes.title: Giants' assault and bloody new race
scenes.summary: The Giants pile mountain upon mountain to reach heaven, and Jupiter hurls lightning and topples them. Earth turns their blood into men, who are as savage as their origin.
scenes.stakes: The Giants risk destruction by Jupiter; Jupiter's rule of heaven is under threat.

place.name: Olympus, Ossa and Pelion

alias_notes.explanation: A title for Jupiter as father and ruler of the gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Ovid says the new men's violence reflects their origin in blood.

analysis.text: Violence and impiety are shown as inherited from the race's origin, continuing the decline of the ages in Book 1 that leads toward the Flood.
The Gigantomachy was a common Greek and Roman image of order defeating chaos, often used to flatter rulers.

legacy.text: The Giants' assault on heaven, piling Pelion on Ossa, gave rise to the proverbial phrase 'to pile Pelion on Ossa' for a huge, excessive effort.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's account ties the Gigantomachy to the mythic origin of humanity's cruelty, a variation on other myths of creation.

language_notes.text: "Æther" is the pure, bright upper air where the gods dwell, distinct from the lower air men breathe.
Olympus, Ossa and Pelion are mountains in northern Greece. Olympus was the gods' home; the Giants stacked Ossa on Pelion to climb toward it.
"Lest no memorial... should be surviving" is an archaic double negative; it means she wished some remembrance of her sons to survive.
"You might see" is a generalizing address to the reader, meaning anyone could tell their savage nature came from their bloody origin.

context_notes.text: Jupiter is the king of the gods and wielder of the thunderbolt. Here he defends heaven against the Giants, children of Earth.
Earth (Terra, Gaia in Greek) was mother of the Giants, so she makes new humans from her slain sons' blood.

literary_notes.text: "They say" distances the narrator from the story and signals that he reports tradition, not eyewitness fact.
Drenched earth and warm gore make a vivid, visceral picture of life springing from slaughter.
The new humans' bloodthirst, tied to their origin, prepares for Lycaon's crime and the coming flood.
